images.caption: Burial ground near Fishguard. This 20th century burial ground is located alongside a minor road about half a mile beyond Fishguard, looking north east the hills and coast. Several members of one family buried here lie within sight of their own farm, Cilshafe Fawr, directly across the valley.

images.filename: Enjoying the view at the Gorsedd circle, Fishguard - geograph.org.uk - 217410.jpg
images.caption: Enjoying the view at the Gorsedd circle, Fishguard. This Gorsedd (throne) circle of stones remains from the Crowning of the Bard at the 1936 eisteddfod held at Fishguard/Abergwaun. It was famously the occasion of a drunken visit by Augustus John and Dylan Thomas who fell out to such an extent that the young poet was turned out of the car on the way back.

images.caption: Fern (Dryopteris affinis) architecture, near to Fishguard/Abergwaun, Pembrokeshire/Sir Benfro, Wales. The fronds fan out from the cluster of rhizomes at the base, maximising their exposure to sunlight. A familiar sight in spring woodland and one that has been around a long time. Ferns have been in existence since the Early Carboniferous period about 300 million years

images.caption: Cable cottage near Parcymorfa This tiny stone building started out (I believe) as a underwater cable terminal and was later associated with a bowling green located here. Now its original footprint has been extended at the rear to create a self-catering cottage with a magnificent view over Fishguard Harbour.

images.filename: Bird on the wire, stonechat - geograph.org.uk - 872249.jpg
images.caption: Bird on the wire: stonechat Saxicola rubicola. A small bird with a rasping call like two pebbles being clashed together: the sound is inescapable along the coast, as here, and they are often to be seen on top of gorse bushes and other vantage points. The stonechat breeds in the west and south of the British Isles. This is a male with its striking patch of red on the chest and a black head.

images.caption: Common Mallow (Malvia sylvestris) Often found around old buildings as here in the ruins of Fishguard fort.  The flowers are beautifully marked with purple streaks, as if with a paintbrush.  The mucilaginous leaves are edible and can be used in cooking for thickening soups and stews (especially in Egypt as melokhia), and also medically for gut-soothing.

images.caption: Common toadflax (Linaria vulgaris) The curiously shaped flower gives rise to the name 'cod's head' in Norwegian, and in dialect nomenclature it has been likened to a variety of other animals' mouths:  dog, rabbit, mouse, lion, monkey and so on. Its colouration accounts for the alternative English name of butter-and-eggs; the eggyolk-orange part gets darker as it matures. The plant can become very invasive and is regarded as a weed. Being hard to distinguish amongst true flax until it flowered it was awarded a pejorative affiliation with toads.
